v.why: Filling an empty node2->output edge with a 3x3 conv creates a new learnable path, a much bigger gain than swapping out an existing op (exp 4).
Adding a conv on the missing direct input->output edge adds a whole new path, unlike replacing an existing skip (exp 13 vs exp 1).
Without the node1->output edge, the direct edge is one of very few paths to the output, so removing it is especially damaging (exp 10).
With edge 1 absent, removing edge 0 cuts node 2 off from the input too, collapsing the cell to at most the direct edge (exp 18).
When edge 0 is none, node 1 outputs zeros, so a conv on node1->node2 cannot add the benefit it normally does.
When node 1 is dead because edge 0 is none, upgrading the node1->output edge has no effect on accuracy.
Replacing parameter-free pooling on the final edge with a 3x3 conv gains more than replacing a 1x1 conv (exp 6).
Adding a conv where the input->node2 edge was missing creates a new deep path, so the gain exceeds an op swap.
Adding a residual connection where none existed greatly improves trainability, while swapping a conv for skip on that edge is roughly neutral.
With no direct input->output edge, removing node2->output removes a large share of the remaining paths to the output (exp 16).

raw:
I picked these hypotheses using the 20 experiments plus how this search space is wired.

**Main patterns:**
- **Replacing `none` adds a new path.** When the parent edge is `none`, adding a convolution or skip helps more than swapping one op for another. Experiments 4 and 13 show this (+3.5 to +8 pp).
- **Removing an edge hurts more when the cell has few other paths.** Experiments 10, 16 and 18 show losses of 6–17 pp when the removed edge carried most of the signal.
- **Edges leaving node 1 do nothing when edge 0 is `none`.** Node 1 then outputs zeros, so edits to edges 2 and 4 have little or no effect.
- **Pooling to convolution is a big gain; convolution to pooling is a big loss.** Experiment 14 shows the loss side (−4 to −14 pp).
